title_en: The Brahma of the World of Illusion (Maya)
translation:
The Brahma of the World (Maya)

The Children Were Brought Back — In the satsang, on the tenth day of the bright half of Chaitra in Samvat 1710, Jivanji Maharaj discussed the episode of the Brahmin's children as it appears in the Bhagavatam.

The satsang held on the tenth day of the bright half of Chaitra in Samvat 1710 told of a Brahmin near Dwarka whose children, one after another, would not survive birth. The child would be born, live only long enough for its mother and father to see its face, and then it would vanish. This caused the Brahmin great sorrow. Then one day Arjun came there. Hearing the story, Arjun said, how could this be? Growing angry at Shri Krishna and Balbhadra, Arjun declared that some demon, gandharva, or yaksha must have carried the child away. If Death (Kaal) had taken it, the Brahmin would have seen the corpse; since no corpse was seen, someone must be carrying the child off whole. In front of Kripanath (Krishna), Arjun declared in the assembly that the duty of a Kshatriya no longer stood. "O Brahmin, your wife now carries her seventh child — when she is about to give birth, call for me," he said, and thus consoled him. Then when the time of birth came, Arjun was sent for. Arjun built such a fortress of arrows — with countless arrows fitted with astras, crosswise, above and below — that he made a cage of arrows around the birthing room in all ten directions, so tight that not even the wind could enter. Yet after the child was born, Arjun did not see it at all — it vanished. Then the wife and husband began to wail in great anguish. "Because this sinner came to watch, we did not even get to see our child's face," they said. "The other children had at least lived a moment, but this one we did not even see." Arjun was crushed in spirit. He then built a pyre and prepared to burn himself upon it. The fifty-six crore Yadavs of Dwarka gathered. Shri Krishna came and gave much counsel, but Arjun would not accept it. Arjun said, "Lord, bring back the Brahmin's children, or I shall burn myself to death on this pyre." Shri Krishna had the chariot yoked; Shri Kripanath himself became the charioteer, and they set out. They pierced through the Himalayas and rose beyond them, passed Lake Manasarovar, crossed Mount Meru and the other great mountains, went past the earth with its seven continents and beyond the realms of the gods and demigods — the oceans and mountains themselves making way for the chariot —

— and thus Arjun and Shri Krishna, crossing Mount Lokalok, reached the great radiant abode of the Lord. At that time, Arjun came to the vicinity of a mountain. From there he saw a great radiance — there was no moon, no sun, no fire. He saw a great effulgence, and there he saw a luminous city of radiant heat. Shri Krishna said, "Halt the chariot here." They stopped the chariot there and walked on. Kripanath took Arjun by the hand and led him there. There stood a fortress, with winding, reversed passages branching out. There, such light emanated as if a thousand veils had been hung. At that doorway it seemed to Arjun that, though looking and looking, he could not see that form at all — but he heard a voice speaking. He saw Shri Krishna speaking, and heard that voice. This form of light, of which one can speak but which cannot be seen because of its intense radiance — no one can truly describe it, such is this incomparable form, it was said. Then, beholding the form of the Parabrahm, they began, with reverence and humility, to bow and offer prayer. Shloka — the words spoken by the mouth of Shri Brahma:

_dadarsha tabhyog sukhasanam vibhum mahanubhavam purushottamottam | sandambudabham supishangavasasam prasannavavratam ruchirayatekshanam ||65||_ (Brahma said: I beheld the Supreme, the greatest of the exalted Purushottamas, seated at ease upon Sheshnag — radiant like a rain-laden cloud, clad in yellow garments, with a serene countenance and beautiful, wide eyes, that form of the Supreme Being who is like the great Kaal.)

Lord Purushottam, reclining upon the body of Sheshnag, was beheld — he was of immense majesty and all-pervading. His radiance was like that of a dense monsoon cloud. He wore beautiful yellow garments; his face was serene, and his eyes were lovely and long.

Brahma said: O Purushottam, you who are the best of all beings, you have done wondrous deeds — you swallowed the forest fire, you humbled Indra's pride. Thus Brahma spoke in wonder — you have accomplished the tasks of many devotees.

_mahamanivratakiritakundalaprabhaparikshiptasahasrakuntalam | pralambachaveshtabhujam rukaustubham shrivatsalakshmam vanamalayavritam ||66||_ (whose hair shone with the radiance of a crown and earrings set with great clusters of gems, whose eight arms were long and beautiful, who wore the Kaustubh gem, bore the mark of Shrivatsa, and wore a garland of forest flowers — such was the Lord I beheld.)

His mass of hair gleamed with the radiance of a crown set with many great gems and of his earrings. He had eight arms, long and graceful. He wore the Kaustubh gem at his throat, and was adorned with a forest garland that enhanced the beauty of his Shrivatsa mark.

The Vedas have sung your great praise, O treasure of mercy (Kripanidhan). Your name is that of the being of a thousand radiant powers. Maharaj, you have accomplished great deeds — you slew Trinavart, Pralambasur, Bakasur, Vatsasur, Dhenukasur, Aghasur, Shankhasur, Mushtik, Chanur, Keshi, and Kansa; you have performed mighty feats of valor. You bear these marks in fullness, Lakshmi serves you, and you wear a forest garland at your throat. To you, who are such a Lord, I bow.

_sunandapramukhaih svaparshadaishchakradibhirmurtidharainijayudhai | pushtya shriya kirtyajayakhilardhibhirnishevyamanam parimeshthinam patim ||67||_ (I beheld the Lord of all the exalted ones, attended by his own companions headed by Sunanda and Nanda, by his own weapons — the discus and others — which had taken bodily form, and served by Pushti, Shri, Kirti, Ajaya, and all manner of divine prosperities.)

His companions, chief among them Sunanda and Nanda, his own embodied weapons such as the discus, and Pushti, Lakshmi, Kirti, Maya, and the eight siddhis all attended upon him in service. Beholding this Lord reclining upon Shesh, Arjun and Shri Krishna grew awed, and stood with joined hands, bowing to the Lord who is the master of all great souls and their own very source. To them, that all-pervading Lord — the Lord even of lords — spoke in a grave voice as follows.

_vavanda atmanamanantamachyutam jishnushcha tadarshanajatasadhvasah | tavaha bhuma parameshthinam prabhurbaddhanjali sasmitamurjaya gira ||68||_ (Krishna and Arjun, who had grown awestruck at the sight of the Lord, bowed with devotion to that Infinite, Imperishable One. To the two of them, standing with joined hands, the Great Being, the Lord of the exalted ones, spoke smilingly in a majestic voice.)

_dvijatmaja me yuvayordidakshuna mayopanita bhuvi dharmaguptyai | kalavatirnavavanerbharasuran hatved bhuyastvarayetamanti me ||69||_ (These sons of the Brahmin were brought here by me for the sake of protecting Dharma in the world — the reason being that I desired to see the two of you. You who have descended as partial incarnations, having slain the demons who had become a burden upon the earth, come to me quickly, both of you.)

The Purna Purushottam (the Total Being) said: Out of my desire to see you, I brought the Brahmin's sons here. Both of you have incarnated from a portion of Myself to relieve the earth of its burden and to protect Dharma. Now, having finished the task of slaying the demons who burden the earth, come to me.

O Maharaj, your divine play is here on this earth. Having taken leave of me you departed, yet that bound of order is never broken. When he fell into deep sorrow, you went and brought back the Brahmin's children. Showing great mercy toward me, you left that play behind and came here. O Maharaj, I who am your very portion — how am I? I fill all three worlds, and yet I had become diminished, for that portion of me which separated when you took incarnation had gone apart from me. So by coming here you have done a great deed. Do come again soon — my heart ever dwells upon you.

_purnakamavapi yuvam naranarayanavrishi | dharmaacharatam sthityai rishabhau lokasangraham ||60||_ (Though you two, Nara and Narayan, are ever complete in yourselves and desire nothing, being the foremost of sages, you must continue to practice Dharma for the sake of upholding the world's order — for the guidance of humankind.)

_ityadishtau bhagavata tau krishnau parameshthina | omityanamya bhumanamadaya dvijadvarakan ||61|| nyavartatam svakam dhama sampradrishtau yathagatam | viprya dadatuh putran yatharupam yathavayah ||62||_

Thus commanded by the all-pervading Purna Purushottam Bhagavan, both Shri Krishna and Arjun, gladly accepting his command, took the Brahmin's sons, bowed to the all-pervading Purna Purushottam Bhagavan, and returned by the same path they had come, back to Dwarka. There they gave the Brahmin his sons, restored to exactly the same form and age as before.

_nishamya vaishnavam dhama parthah paramavismitah | yatkinchitam paurusham pusam mene krishnanukampitam ||63||_

(Having beheld the abode of Vishnu, Arjun was struck with the greatest wonder, and he came to understand that whatever valor or achievement a man possesses is entirely due to the grace of the Lord.)

The Lord's radiance, like that of ten million suns, resides in his lotus feet themselves.

Then Arjun asked Kripanath, "What was that conversation about?" Shri Krishna replied, "He told me, 'You are welcome; I am waiting for you — come soon.' And I told him, 'I am still attending to the work of creation, and will come.'" Thus did the gentle Kripanath conduct himself in this matter concerning Arjun. Such was Arjun's fraternal intimacy (sakha-bhaav, the disposition of treating the Lord as an equal companion) toward Krishna that it undid him entirely, root and all — it did him harm. Because of the arrogance that arose in Arjun, Krishna had to undergo the trouble of bringing back the Brahmin's children in order to save him.

_vishvasah samatanityam sakhyatam bhava uchyate_ — (Trust that is always accompanied by a sense of equality is called sakhya-bhaav, the disposition of friendship-as-equals.)

Jivandasji said: whoever holds such a disposition does not fare well. Because Arjun held this sakha-bhaav toward Shri Krishna, this misfortune befell him.

_kabir paarath shooro me sunyo | jaake saarangpaan sahaay | baaher veri bohot hune | ek na maarya maanhi ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: I have heard that Parth was such a great warrior that the Lord himself aided him. Yet though he slew many outer enemies of the world, he did not slay even the one inner enemy — the ego.)

_paarath shoora me sunya | krishna arjunki saakh | harikee paarakh na padi | gaya himalaya dakh ||_ (Prem Bhakt says: I have heard that Arjun was such a great warrior, and that there was a sakha-bhaav between Krishna and Arjun. Yet, because he failed to recognize that Krishna was truly Bhagwan, he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones. Behold this example of what happened between Krishna and Arjun.)

_kabir dehithe dehi mili | suno krishna arjunki saakh | shabd ki paarakh na padi | gaye himale dakh || shabd vichaare baahare | sadguru shabd jaanya vina ||_

(Das Kabirji says: an embodied soul met an embodied form of God — hear this example of Krishna and Arjun. But he failed to recognize the teaching of the World-Guru Krishna, and so acted contrary to Krishna's teaching; behold, therefore, he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones.)

Arjun was an embodied being, and Krishna too had manifested by taking on a body, but Krishna was God himself — so although he had a body, he was beyond the body. Yet Arjun regarded Krishna merely as an embodied being, and so could not accept him as his Guru. In the Gita, chapter 2, verse 7, though Arjun did say, "Shishyaste'ham shaadhi maam tvaam prapannam" (I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you, in whatever is good for me), still he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones — thus his conduct turned away from Krishna's spoken teaching. Therefore, one should not regard the Guru as merely a bodily being.

_je sajaniya sukh podhate | so jan gaye kedar | guru shabd bin jivana | mile na dooji vaar ||157||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: those Pandavs who once enjoyed the comfort of being close kin to Lord Krishna nonetheless went to Kedar in the Himalayas to have their bones ground down. This was because they had not received the teaching of a true Guru; hence, in the Himalayas, a World-Guru like Shri Krishna, one who could give them teaching such as the Gita again, was not to be found there a second time.)

Poojya Yadunath, in Litiyu No. 67, page 10, writes concerning this episode that Jivanji Maharaj said of Arjun: Arjun, who used to sleep in the same bed as Lord Krishna, went to Kedar to die at the time of his death without ever having recognized the Lord — and this itself shows that he had not known Krishna for who he truly was.

_krishna sameepi pandava | gale himalaya jaay | loha ko paaras mile | kaahe kaayi khaay ||26||_ (In the Bijak, Das Kabirji says: even though the Pandavs lived close to Krishna, they went to the Himalayas and had their bones ground away. For if iron has truly touched the philosopher's stone, it turns to gold — and how then could rust consume it? In the same way, since these Pandavs failed to recognize Krishna, they fell into the ocean of worldly existence.)

In a composition named Sharanlila, Bhagwandas has written:

_maara vahaala sevak jan | ek sajyaaye sen kare | ekatha kare bhojan | ek ekane kautuk kare | maahara vahaala_ (Bhagwan says: My devoted servants are very dear to me. I sleep together with them in the same bed, I take meals together with them, and I even engage in playful roughhousing with them. Thus did he behave with the Pandav Arjun.)

Among the Pandavs who set out on the great ascent toward heaven to have their bones ground away, when Arjun's body finally gave out, Bhim asked Yudhishthir: according to the law of the wheel of time, even Arjun Parth has fallen — how could such a famed archer, the wielder of the Gandiv bow, leave us and go? Yudhishthir replied that he was a proud and willful archer, and that was why he fell. Thus, the pride he displayed in the episode of bringing back the Brahmin's children was shown here.

This is discussed in Gujarat Samachar, 24 January 2002, page 11.

It was stated in the satsang that because Arjun held sakha-bhaav toward Krishna, no true good came of it, for he went to Kedar to be ground away — a place considered to be Shivji's domain. Jivanji Maharaj himself went there and, upon returning, concluded that this was no fit place for any devotee of the Lord to dwell; and so he turned back from there. Shivji is the form of Omkar, while the saints and devotees are the rightful heirs of the Lord's realm beyond the three gunas. Hence, a sakhi is quoted here describing Omkar.

_manasa devi upani | taathe bhaya omkaar | ghat ghat vyaapak jivana | so khele nandadwaar ||1||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says, in the section named Garbhavati, concerning the soul entangled in the wheel of 8.4 million species: at the beginning of creation, a goddess named Mansa, of the nature of Maya, arose, and from her the Omkar-bound creation came into being. That very essence of the Parabrahm Paramatma pervades every single body in this world — and that Supreme Being sports in the courtyard of Nandji.)

_ichchha (manasa) roopi naari avatari | taaka naam gaayatri dhari | taake teen bhaye jo pootaa | brahma vishnu mahadev suta ||_ (In the Ramaini of the Bijak, Das Kabirji says: a woman in the form of Desire, that is Goddess Mansa, came into being, and she was given the name Gayatri. She bore three sons — Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj instructed us to practice bhakti toward Vishnu, but this is not that Vishnu born of Gayatri — rather, it is the beginningless, endless, complete Parabrahm Paramatma, through whom this creation of the illusory world was made.)

Reference: Hindu Dharmakosh, page 493 — "Among the many forms of the Mansa-shakti, worship of the goddess named Mansa is very prevalent in Bengal. A good number of songs in her praise have also been composed, known collectively by the literary name 'Mansamangal.' She is regarded as the mother of serpents, and her worship is believed to ward off trouble from snakes." Mansa-vrat: Goddess Mansa should be worshipped on the ninth day of the bright half of Jyeshtha when conjoined with the Hasta lunar asterism, or, absent that conjunction, on the tenth day, upon a branch of the Snuhi tree. According to Hemadri, in the Chaturvarga Chintamani, part one, page 621, the worship of Goddess Mansa should take place on the fifth day of the dark half of Ashadh. Mansa is also worshipped on the eleventh day of the dark half of Shravan. (From a book titled Bhasha tatha Sahitya, pages 257-276.)

Mansadevi — a goddess of this name has her temple atop the mountain behind Har-ki-Pauri in Haridwar. She is the mind-born daughter of Sage Kashyap, and the wife of Jaratkaru (Mahabharat, Adi Parva, chapters 45-48 and 160): sister of Vasuki, she is the queen of serpents. She is also called Jagadgaura, Nitya, and Padmavati. She is regarded as a portion of the root Prakriti and a beloved disciple of Sadashiv. She is worshipped as the goddess who protects against fearsome crawling creatures. Her nature is jealous — if she is not worshipped first, she sends snakes to take revenge.

Kabir has mentioned her in a pad, in Raga Asavari:

_santo bhai dhokha sabku maare | ko niramal gyaan vichaare ||tek|| koi khoje shiv shaktiku | koo khoje kaaya | koo khoje shoonya mandalku | aise jug bharmaaya ||1|| koo mansa khojai | ko ulata pavan chalaavai | koo khoje jantra mantraku | koo kaashi chal jaavai ||2|| koo jangam jalme naahaavai | koo shekh shayaana | koo desh deshaantar dolai | koo tap teerath lapataana ||3|| bharam karamki saankal kaatau | paarabrahmaku sevai | kahat kabir so harikaa daasaa | maathe boj na levai ||4||_

(Das Kabirji says: O brother saints, delusion and deceit destroy everyone; only a rare few of truly pure understanding grasp this. Others strive to find the Supreme Reality through the practice of Shiv-Shakti; some strive to search for it within the body through knowledge of Brahm; some try to find it through Goddess Mansa; others practice yoga, holding the breath through pranayam; some seek it in tantric rites and mantras; some go off to the region of Kashi; some bathe in the water of a Shiva-linga; some become clever dilettantes; some wander from land to land; some are lured into the trap of austerities and pilgrimage. But whoever breaks the bonds of superstition, delusion, and karma and worships the Parabrahm Paramatma alone is called a true devotee of the Parabrahm Paramatma — such a one no longer accepts the bondage of karma.)

The hidden, subtle form of Desire is Vasana (latent craving), and the subtler form of Vasana is Sanskar (impression); that is to say, the manifest form of Sanskar is Vasana, the gross form of Vasana is Desire, and the gross form of Desire is sorrow and delusion.

In Raga Asavari:

_manchha maalani re | tu soorat chhaabari leh | jal ban koop bhom ban baari | aradh uradh beech kyaari || ihaanke phool uhaan pahonchaaye | so maalan piya pyaari ||1|| moj dei maalan paheraai | baso apana bheeraa | shoon shikhar gadh leeo mukaate | gaave daas kabeeraa ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: O Mansa, you flower-seller woman, you go about carrying a basket of attentive, focused meditation. Your flower-garden has neither water nor well; there is a bed of flowers set in the space between above and below. You take the flowers grown there and deliver them elsewhere, O beloved gardener-woman of the Beloved. Delighted, the flower-seller garlands everyone with her garlands and then, in fear, withdraws to abide in her own place. Das Kabirji, having settled in the highest state of effortless samadhi, sings the praises of the Lord's qualities.)

Parth and the Pandavs, too, were destroyed by just such delusion and deceit. A sakhi is now given, introducing the Parabrahm — the source from whom this delusion arises.

_kabir antariksh ida agamka | adhar raha niraadhaar | nitya vikase nirmaan phal | trigun vriksh vistaar ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: the sphere of the unfathomable Brahm-essence of the Lord's nature cannot be known; it abides fixed without any support at all. It ever unfolds and continually produces fruit. Such is this tree, whose spread has extended into the three gunas.)

Ida means one egg — one portion out of the infinite cosmos.

_kabir sava lakh niramaan | uthe nitya avaaz | lakh sabad samata same | rahat anaamat gaaz ||3||_

Niranjan (Dharmaray) performed austerities and demanded sovereignty over the three worlds, the ocean of worldly existence. Growing arrogant because of this, he received a curse: from now on you shall no longer have sight of Me; and every day you shall swallow up a hundred thousand souls and give birth to a hundred and twenty-five thousand. The Lord's supreme devotees, roaring their defiance and confronting Niranjan's challenge every day, go on to the Lord's abode; crossing over Niranjan's dominion of the ocean of worldly existence, they proceed on to reach the Lord.

A Shabd:

_chetho re cheto nar baavare | kaha achet rahaai | kaal daga hai sir oopare | sabku dhar khaai ||1|| lachh jeev nit khaat hai | sava lakh oopai hau | kaahuku chhede nahi | aise kaal anyaai ho ||2|| jagat chavena hai kaalka | sabko khaat yugaai ho | chun chun khaaye shoormaan | khaate na adhaai ho ||3|| kul marjaada metake | karo tum sad sagaai ho | kahai kabir tab bancho | kaal daga mit jaai ho ||4||_

(Das Kabirji says: Oh, you bewildered mortals — how can you remain so unconscious? The treacherous Kaal circles above your heads and seizes and devours everyone. Every day he devours a hundred thousand souls and produces a hundred twenty-five thousand more, yet he spares no one — such a deceiver he is. This whole world is merely a snack for Kaal to munch on, and even so, he is never satisfied. Therefore, cast off the flowery bonds of the Vedas, ritual works, and the like, and bind yourself instead to the true relationship with the Lord's own Name. Only then, Kabir says, will you be able to escape, and the fear of Kaal's treachery will vanish.)

Das Kabirji says (reference: manuscript No. 8, page 228; No. 28, page 191) — a Ramaini:

_kalime niranjan bade anyaayi | ochhe bade jeev sab khaai ||1|| laakh jeevaka kare aahaaraa | sava laakh jeev jug vistaaraa ||2|| aap gapat hoi raho chhipaai | laakh jeev tahaan le maagaai ||3|| apana naam niranjan keena | thakuraai jin aapahi leena ||4|| moorakh jeev kachhu samajata naahi | kahaansu aavai kahaan chal jaavai ||5|| agam panthaka khoj na karahi | phir phir parchaame par hi ||6|| ghatame karataa kaun kahaavai | taahe chhaandi yon dhyaan lagaavai ||7|| man hi vibhram ghatake raajaa | taate saryo na eko kaajaa ||8||_

_man ramataa sab ghatame | suranar muni karo vichaar | kahai kabir tahaan puras hai | jaho shabd takasaar ||64||_ (Sakhi)

(Das Kabirji says: in this Kali Yug, the Nirgun Brahm, the false Niranjan, is a great tyrant, destroying beings both small and great. He kills a hundred thousand souls, and spreads a hundred and twenty-five thousand more into the world. He himself remains hidden, concealed, and from that hiding place summons a hundred thousand souls. He has taken for himself the name Niranjan — free of Maya, the Nirgun Brahm — and has kept lordship over all for himself. Foolish, unwitting souls understand nothing; they do not understand where they have come from nor where they must go. They do not seek out the hidden, unfathomable path, and so fall again and again into the cycle. Abandoning the One who truly governs within the body, they fix their attention here and there instead. Since the mind, the ruler and governor of the body, wanders in delusion, no true good is ever accomplished in any way. Sakhi: the mind revels within every body. O gods, men, and sages, reflect upon this — Kabirji says the Soul dwells right within this very body, where its voice, its sovereign presence, its dwelling, resides and moves.)

Four more sakhis regarding this Niranjan are given below in this ramaini —

_kabir teen chori bhi | sab kaahuka sarabas leen | binaa moodaka chokhaa | paraa na kaahu cheentu ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: theft has occurred in all three worlds — everyone's all has been taken away. Yet no one could ever recognize that headless — that is, having a head, yet without mercy — thief.)

The headless thief refers to Omkar, the Formless Brahm — the mind, Maya, and Desire in the form of a thief. Hanumandas has said of this thief: "Just as, without a head, a trunk cannot be recognized, so too in that binding-free Omkar-essence, the ultimate reality, all worlds dissolve away — yet no one could understand it." The three worlds mean Rajas (the devotee), Tamas (the yogi), and Sattva (the man of knowledge) — theft occurred among all three of these, robbing them entirely, souls and all. By the syllable "U", devotees were robbed; by the syllable "M", yogis were robbed; and by the half-syllable, men of knowledge were robbed — all were deluded. Yet that headless thief, Omkar, was recognized by no one. This Omkar is nothing but a false imagination. Because it went unrecognized in this way, it devoured the whole world. Or else, the headless thief is Desire, who committed theft in all three worlds and took away the understanding of gods, demons, and men alike, subduing them all and imprisoning them in the dark cell of the womb. Bound in this desire, all — Brahma and his kind, Vishnu and his kind, Shiva and his kind — dance to its tune. Yet this thief in the form of Desire was recognized by no one.

Rivanaresh writes: "The headless thief is the formless Brahm, whom no one could recognize; or else, the headless thief refers to the worshippers of the goddess Chhinnamasta, who hold no devotion for anyone else, saying, 'We ourselves have no head — for what reason? Because it is written that one must become the deity to worship the deity.' These Shakta worshippers are recognized by no one; casting all souls into Maya, she keeps them all deluded." Rivanaresh regards either the Formless Brahm, or the goddess whose own head has been severed, as this headless thief. This Shakta goddess is one who takes sacrifice by cutting off the heads of all.

In the text Bhavtaran, it is stated in a chaupai concerning Niranjan:

_dharamdaas suno sant sujaanaa | niragunkaa ab karahu bakhaanaa | niragun naam niranjan bhaai | tin saari utapat banaai || niragunse bhayo ohankaaraa | taaso teeno gun vistaaraa | trigunse man bhayaa prachandaa | taako baas sakal brahmandaa || vo onkaar man aap niranjan | naanaa vidhake kiye veejan | bhaanti bhaatike ghaat sanvaaraa | kahaan lagi kahu vaar na paaraa || taake ansh sakal avataaraa | paraam krishn taame saradaaraa | pooran aap niranjan hoi | iname pherphaar nahi koi || niragun niragunki karai sevaa | bhakti karai aur poojai devaa | karai aachaar vichaar na jaanai | sau mere man kabahu na maanai || man bodhe man maanhi samaavai | nij padakun koi nahi paavai | manakun bodh karai jo koi | man pahuchaavai pahuchai soi || jaay niranjan maanhi samaavai | aage gaman kaahu paavai | aise teen lok sab atakai | khare sayaanai te sab bhatakai || rishi muni gan gandharv devaa | sab mili karai niranjan sevaa | siddh saadhak saadhu jo bhayeu | eenake aage koi na gayeu || bahut preetsu bhagat vichaari | milat milat milai adhikaari | jaay niranjan so hoy bhetaa | kaal roop dhar kare sameta || ehi niranjan ker pasaaraa | taame urajho sab sansaaraa | jaahaan taahaan raakhe vilamaai | rachanaa anant apaar banaai || dharamdaas tum bhakt sanehi | iname jin atakaavau dehi | janam dhare nahi bhaai | taato aayo kahu gauhoraai || bhagat gupat jaane nahi koi | surat dharamdaas sujaan ||_

(O wise saint Dharamdas, listen — now I shall describe the Nirgun. O brother, Nirgun's name is Niranjan; he has fashioned the entire creation of this world. From the Nirgun arose Omkar, and from that the three gunas spread forth. From the three gunas the mind became fierce and forceful, and it dwells throughout the entire cosmos. That Omkar-mind is itself Niranjan; he has produced seeds of many different kinds, fashioned forms of every manner — how far shall I go on describing them, for they have neither end nor limit. All the divine incarnations are but portions of him; among these, Ram and Krishna are foremost. They themselves are the complete Niranjan; in this there is no difference at all. Yet, in their manifest form, they render service and devotion to the Nirgun principle, and worship the gods — they perform such rites and worldly reasonings, but my mind never accepts this. The mind, once instructed, settles back within the mind itself; no one attains their own true state this way. Whoever instructs the mind is carried only as far as the mind can carry him, and no further — he goes and is absorbed into Niranjan alone; none can attain passage beyond that. Thus all three worlds remain stuck there; even the truly wise all wander lost in it. Sages, munis, the hosts of gandharvas and gods — all together render service to Niranjan. Whatever siddhas, sadhaks, and sadhus there have been, none has ever gone beyond him. With great love the devout one reflects, and by meeting again and again, the one who is worthy attains him; he goes and has his meeting with Niranjan, but Niranjan, assuming the form of Kaal, gathers him up. This is the vast expanse of Niranjan, in which the whole world lies entangled; he keeps beings delayed here and there, having fashioned a creation that is endless and boundless. O Dharamdas, you are a loving devotee — do not let your embodied self get caught up in this. [The following line is obscure in the source.] No one knows the secret, hidden devotion — attend closely, O wise Dharamdas.)

Sakhi — _inate gupat bhagat hai | suno dharamdaas sujaan | bhagati karai bhav aavai nahi | soi bhagati pramaan ||_ (There is a truer, hidden devotion beyond this Niranjan — hear it, O wise Dharamdas: that devotion which, once practiced, keeps one from returning to this ocean of worldly existence — that alone is the proof of true devotion.)

_kabir aad purush to ek vriksh hai | niranjan vaaki haar | trigun roop hi shaakhaa bhai | paat bhaye sansaar ||3||_ (variant reading: "Brahma and Vishnu become branches") — (Das Kabirji says: the Original Being, the Supreme Self, is like a single tree, and Niranjan is like a branch of it. The three-gunas forms — Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva — become its branches, and this creation becomes its leaves.)

Kabir has said in a Ramaini (reference: Kuvarpura Grantha No. 7, page 4 / No. 28, page 173):

_niragun pedh aad banvaari | niragunki saragun haari | taa daariika e vistaaraa | raajaa rank sakal sansaaraa || raj veerajaka keenhaa melaa | taatai bhayaa guru aru chelaa | jaamane ek sab jaamaa | ghar beru aru baahar naamaa || ek dehakaa eh anusaaraa | na koo bhayaa kaahute nyaaraa | paanch tataka sab hi bhaande | nahi koi shoodra nahi koi paande || haad chaamakaa ropyaa thambhaa | taamai duniyaa karai aarambhaa || ek hi deevalaa ekahi joti | pandit karau kaunki chhoti ||_

_kabi pandit chhot na keejie | dekho soch vichaar | ham tum ekahi jaat hai | gharani amar mojhaar ||1||_

(Das Kabirji says: the root tree of the Garland-Bearer, the Lord, is the Nirgun; the sagun devotion serves that Nirgun. The branches of that tree have spread out, and within them lies the whole world — kings and paupers alike. Through the union of seed and blood, guru and disciple alike have come into being. All the bodies held within the womb-fluid are bodies of this kind; one's household and one's separate outer lineage all conform to this same single kind of body — none has been made different from another. All are pots molded from the same five elements; among them there is no Shudra, and no Pandit-Brahmin either. These pillars of bone and skin have been erected, bodies have been fashioned, and it is dwelling within them that the world begins its work. Since it is thus all of one and the same kind, then why, O learned Brahmins, do you practice this defilement of untouchability through touch? O Pandits, do not shrink back in this fear of pollution — reflect deeply, just for a moment, and see that you and we belong to one and the same kind, dwelling together upon this same eternal earth.)

_kabir chor ham bhal olakhiyaa | chor keenahu na keen | chor paramodhe jagataku | choraku hamahi dakhyaa deen ||4||_ (Das Kabirji says: it is good that we recognized the thieves, for the thieves have not been able to do us the slightest harm. These thieves go about giving the people of the world instruction and understanding. But we have taught such thieves a proper lesson.
